subject: giant sinkhole
title: What If the Ground Swallowed a Building? Guatemala City's Did in 2010

scenes.text: What if the ground under a city block just vanished? In Guatemala City, it did.
End of May 2010. After Tropical Storm Agatha's deluge, a hole opened downtown and swallowed a three-storey building.
About 18 metres across and 100 metres deep. Thirty storeys straight down, with almost vertical walls.
There's no limestone under the city, so it wasn't a natural sinkhole. The ground is loose pumice from ancient volcanic eruptions.
Geologist Sam Bonis says a burst sewer or storm drain probably washed that pumice away for years, hollowing a cavern until the roof gave way.
A hole just like it had opened five kilometres away in 2007. A report warned more would come unless the sewers were inspected. The government never replied.

description:
What if the ground under a city block simply disappeared? At the end of May 2010, after Tropical Storm Agatha, a hole about 18 metres wide and 100 metres deep opened in downtown Guatemala City and swallowed a three-storey building.
Geologists said it was not a true sinkhole: the city sits on loose pumice from past eruptions rather than limestone, and a leaking sewer or storm drain had probably washed the material away over years until the roof of the cavity collapsed. Dartmouth geologist Sam Bonis had co-authored a report after a similar hole opened 5 km away in 2007, warning that more would follow unless the sewer system was inspected.
